newsitem.title: FRANCE: Ranariddh warns of civil war in Cambodia.
newsitem.headline: Ranariddh warns of civil war in Cambodia.

text.p: Ousted Cambodian First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh warned on Tuesday that a new civil war could ravage his homeland if his rival Hun Sen refused to negotiate Ranariddh's return to power.

"I am willing to see Hun Sen to solve this problem in an existing legal framework, but if we cannot, there would be, alas, a civil war in my poor country," Ranariddh, the son of King Sihanouk, told a news conference in Paris.
In Phnom Penh, the Cambodian interior ministry said a senior official from Ranariddh's party was shot dead after being arrested by troops loyal to Second Prime Minister Hun Sen.
Ho Sok, a secretary of state at the Interior Ministry, was arrested on Monday and later killed, Interior Ministry advisor Khieu Sopheak, a member of Hun Sen's party, told reporters.

Ranariddh was toppled at the weekend by Cambodia's second prime minister who had shared power with him in an ungainly two-headed coalition government formed after a United Nations-run election in the Southeast Asian nation in 1993.

Hun Sen had accused Ranariddh of smuggling defectors into the capital from the Khmer Rouge guerrilla group, whose brutal 1975-79 "killing fields" regime caused the deaths of more than one million Cambodians.
Ranariddh in turn accused Hun Sen of staging a coup d'etat against him to sabotage elections scheduled for 1998.

At his Paris news conference, Ranariddh urged world powers not to recognise Hun Sen's new regime and said he was going to the United States on Wednesday to speak to the U.N. Security Council and later to U.S. Vice-President Al Gore or Secretary of State Madeleine Albright.
"I am asking the international community to take a clear position and to never recognise a government resulting from a coup d'etat," he told reporters.

Ranariddh said Phnom Penh no longer qualified for international assistance as it no longer met the demands of donor nations and institutions which pledged $450 million in aid to Cambodia in Paris last week.
The donors had asked the government to ensure that the gains made since 1993 were not undermined by political instability.
Hun Sen, however, told the international community on Tuesday to stay out of Cambodia's affairs, saying the people should be left alone to sort out their problems.
Ranariddh fled Cambodia for France last Friday, a day before the outbreak of the fighting between his troops and forces loyal to Hun Sen which led to his ouster.
Hun Sen accused Ranariddh of teaming up with Khmer Rouge deserters.

Ranariddh denied he was in contact with the guerrilla group but said that if they fought on his behalf in Cambodia, "there is nothing I can do about that. I have no contact with them, I have no link with them."
Ranariddh said the international community should grant asylum to members of his FUNCINPEC party and its allies who he said were being persecuted by the new regime.
"There is a genuine witch-hunt being conducted by Hun Sen's men. I want to draw the attention of the international community to the extreme danger faced by our members."
